messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Random Walk with covariates
messages.body_plain:
its only implemented for AR1 at the moment.

note that the formulation in AR1C is slighly different from
AR1+covariates, as you directly change the innovations in  AR1C, where
in AR1+covariates you alter the mean only.

you can add this yourself, using R, with rgeneric, or even add your own
C code.

see the vignette about rgeneric

messages.body_plain:
Yes, this is all with constr=TRUE, but with the default intercept=0 and a sd=10. The intercept used for the simulation is -8. I tested further cases with varying priors on the intercept. All models with "flexible" priors on the intercept seem problematic (although an sd of 2 for the prior on the intercept is not very flexible). Using very thight priors leads to OK models, but that's even with a mean.linear=+10  far way from "truth" and prec.linear=1/0.1^2. I show the sd since I find it a bit more intuitive. All with constr=TRUE and VB enabled. If I disable VB, all models look OK, either with constr=TRUE or FALSE. The code is attached below if needed.

François

messages.subject: simulation from gamma distribution
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community,
I want to validate my model by simulating data from it and compare it with the observations. In inla.doc("gamma") documents I see that the gamma distribution needs the follwing input variables: y = rgamma(n, shape = a, scale = b), whereby
a = prec.par * prec.scale
b = mu / (prec.par * prec.scale)
prec.scale = runif(n, min = 0.5, max = 2)
prec.par = 1.2

I use the "Precision parameter for the Gamma observations" (one of the available hyperpars of the model) for prec.par, but I cannot find what I should use for prec.scale? Is this something specific per model simulation or something else?
Regards, Bram

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] lgcp not working well with experimental mode
messages.body_plain:
The interplay with the smooth and the intercept is the issue, and the
model gives to many options for interpretation.

I added an emergency option, so that these cases would be detected and
then the vb.correction will be disabled (and no correction done).

https://github.com/hrue/r-inla/commit/b040ac0e5db64e51b7d004dbc88012d90fc86572

it will be available in the next build. Let me know if this does not
work well (ps: you can set the 'emergecy' value in the control.vb, and
it to back-off if max|mean[i] - mean.old[i]|/ sd[i] > emergency (this is
checked at each iteration)

thank you François, this discussion (and your examples) were very
useful!

Best
H

messages.subject: Barrier Model ignoring range?
messages.body_plain:
I've been working on a model of a river. The specification for the model is nearly identical to the barrier model in Krainski et al 2020 (ch 5), but using non-separable time as a grouping effect (like ch 7).

The barrier is defined as:
MatRange depends upon the exact run, but varies between 100 and 1000 m, all of which  result in identical looking output figures. At present, MatSig is set at 1/2 MatRange. The attached figure happens to have been generated with a range of 500 m.

barrier.model=inla.barrier.pcmatern(mesh,barrier.triangles=barrier.tri,
    prior.range=c(MatRange,0.5),
    prior.sigma=c(MatSig,0.05) )
inlamode="experimental"
inla.setOption(num.threads=NCore, inla.mode=inlamode, mkl=TRUE)

spde=barrier.model
iset=inla.spde.make.index('i',n.spde=spde$f$n,n.group=k)
A=inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh,loc=coordinates(sensorData.sp),group=sensorData.sp$nt2hour)

formula=y~0+Intercept+f(i,model=spde,group=i.group,control.group=list(model='rw2',cyclic=TRUE, hyper=hyperprec, scale.model=FALSE, adjust.for.con.comp=TRUE))

computelist=list(dic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, q=FALSE, waic=TRUE, smtp="pardiso", graph=FALSE, config=FALSE, mlik=FALSE, return.marginals=FALSE, return.marginals.predictor=FALSE, po=FALSE, hyperpar=FALSE, openmp.strategy="huge")
controlinla=list(int.strategy="eb") #,strategy="gaussian")

res.hrBarrier=inla(formula,
    data=inla.stack.data(sdat),
    control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE, A=inla.stack.A(sdat)),
    inla.mode=inlamode,
    family="gaussian",
    control.inla=controlinla,
    control.family=list(hyper=list(theta=prec.prior)),
    control.compute=computelist,
    num.threads=NCore
    )

For some reason, all outcomes look very similar, with a homogeneous field of 0s at all mesh points except those directly adjacent to my sensor locations (this may be difficult to see in the low-res jpg -- I can attache an SVG if needed, it's just large). This pattern does not change, regardless of what I do with my range in barrier.model.

 My gut is telling me it's because of how long/skinny the sample region is, or am I missing something?

I plot the result exactly as done in ch7 of Karinski et al.

Any recommendations?

Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Barrier Model ignoring range?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

That’s a really difficult domain to work with.
For the barrier model to work as intended there, you will need to have enough triangles to get multiple triangles across the narrow width, I.e. the inner max.edge for the mesh needs to be clearly smaller than the width.

I’m not sure what you mean by MatSig being half MatRange; they control completely different aspects of the covariate (std.dev <http://std.dev>. and spatial range) and you also use different probabilities in the specification.

Getting the same results for different MatRange could mean simply that the data is informative enough to overrule the prior. But I would start by looking at the mesh, to ensure that it’s sufficient to represent the model properly.
I assume you use inla.nonconvex.hull() to construct the outer mesh boundary?

Finn

messages.body_plain:
I appreciate the help.

I've tried a ton of values for the standard deviation, ranging from very small, to my latest attempt  -- 1/2 the range.
I think at some point, I mistakenly interpreted it to be the standard deviation of the range, which doesn't make sense since the probability is specified.
Now that I've actually thought about it, I will use a more sensible value.

The mesh was generated using inla.mesh.2d:

boundary <- list(
as.inla.mesh.segment(land.sp),
    NULL)

mesh.loc <- sensors.sp
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc=mesh.loc,
                     boundary=boundary,
                     max.edge=c(10, 100),
                     min.angle=c(30, 21),
                     max.n=c(48000, 16000), ## Safeguard against large meshes.
                     max.n.strict=c(128000, 128000), ## Don't build a huge mesh!
                     cutoff=2, ## Filter away adjacent points.
                     offset=c(12, 60),
                     crs='EPSG:6417'
)

sensor.sp is the sensor locations, the boundary using a land shape that is larger than the study reach.

I basically create barrier by removing the water area from the land:
land.water.sp=gDifference(land.sp, water.sp)

water.tri=inla.over_sp_mesh(x=land.water.sp, y=mesh, type="centroid", ignore.CRS=TRUE)
water.tri.num=length(mesh$graph$tv[,1])
barrier.tri=setdiff(1:water.tri.num, water.tri)
poly.barrier=inla.barrier.polygon(mesh, barrier.triangles=barrier.tri)

barrier.model=inla.barrier.pcmatern(mesh,barrier.triangles=barrier.tri,
prior.range=c(MatRange,0.5),
prior.sigma=c(MatSig,0.05) )

I believe this followed the example in Krainski ch 5. Should I be using the nonconvex hull instead?

That's good to know, thank you. I may need to revisit the covariance.

Thanks for the prompt reply.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Barrier Model ignoring range?
messages.body_plain:
I would use inla.nonconvex.hull to construct the outer mesh boundary instead of using the default convex hull extension. The convex hull extension has a shape that doesn’t really match the domain of interest. The inner boundary could also likely be made more similar to the actual domain shape.
But the resolution of the inner part looks like it may be sufficient.
However, I’m not sure having the sensor locations as mesh nodes helps or hinders.
Try making the mesh without giving it the sensor locations, so that it only uses the specified boundary/boundaries.
Also, run the model with a regular pcmatern model to see what happens. (Just make sure the outer boundary isn’t too close to the domain of interest.)

Finn

Our cluster is about to go down for maintenance, so I just re-did the mesh without the sensor locations specified (as re-doing the entire mesh would be more time consuming). Regardless, I will report back. I will experiment with non-convex hull after the scheduled maintenance is complete next week.

> I would use inla.nonconvex.hull to construct the outer mesh boundary instead of using the default convex hull extension. The convex hull extension has a shape that doesn’t really match the domain of interest. The inner boundary could also likely be made more similar to the actual domain shape.
> But the resolution of the inner part looks like it may be sufficient.
> However, I’m not sure having the sensor locations as mesh nodes helps or hinders.
> Try making the mesh without giving it the sensor locations, so that it only uses the specified boundary/boundaries.
> Also, run the model with a regular pcmatern model to see what happens. (Just make sure the outer boundary isn’t too close to the domain of interest.)
>
> Finn

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >

> > > > > > >

This pattern does not change, regardless of what I do with my range in barrier.model.
> > > > > > >

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Barrier Model ignoring range?
messages.body_plain:
We have not considered any non-separable covariance/precision model in the SPDE book. What we have there are spatio-temporal (some use to say interaction) models based on the Kronecker product of the precision/covariance between temporal and spatial ones that gives separable precision/covariance.

The terminology problem starts when one uses the inseparability at the mean level (u_{st} cannot splits into u_s + u_t) of the spatio-temporal (interaction: u_{st}) models and gets confused with non-separable precision/covariance (non-separability at a second order property of the model). Thus what we have in the book are spatio-temporal interaction (inseparability at the mean level) but separable precision/covariance models.

The good news is that we are close to having a class of non-stationary and non-separable models implemented and available for the users.

best regards,
Elias

messages.body_plain:
Hi Prof Rue,

Appreciate your valuable suggestions with simple example (runme4.R). That works fine. However, I do not understand whether 'p' values (if I am right these are PITs)  from the posterior samples are for the 'test data' OR for the 'entire data'. When I checked the 'p' values, I found it was available for the 'entire data set'. I am interested in assessing the predictive performance (in terms of PIT histograms) of different models corresponding to 'test data'. Kindly let me know, whether I can draw the PIT histogram corresponding to the 'test data' and if so how can I filter the P values for the test data. The relevant codes from your simple example are given below for your quick reference:

## compute PIT values, the easy (approximative) way. we compuare with the cpo/pit values which
## are not the same (since data are remove), but its about the same with a lot of data (and a
## simple model like here).

xx <- inla.posterior.sample(1000, r)
fun <- function(E, Y) {
    ## theta[1] is 'size',  this must be verified from 'summary(r)'
    size <- theta[1]
    prob <- size / (size + E * exp(Predictor))
    return (pnbinom(Y, size = size, prob = prob))
}
## here we insert complete data
p <- rowMeans(inla.posterior.sample.eval(fun, xx, E = E, Y = y))
plot(p, r$cpo$pit, pch = 19)
abline(a = 0, b = 1, lwd = 3, col = "blue")
hist(p,  breaks=10,main="test data",xlab="PIT")

Once gain thanks a lot for your great help!

ssubra

Hi team

I am a bit confused by syntax to get BLUP values with spde model, for example:

 linharange= range(dat$linha,na.rm=T)
    colunarange= range(dat$coluna,na.rm=T)

    spde= inla.spde2.matern(mesh=mesh,alpha=2)

    stk.e=inla.stack(tag='est',data=list(peso=dat$peso),
                        A=list(A,1,1,1),

m2spde=inla(formula = as.formula(fspde),  data = inla.stack.data(stk.e),

> In inlabru you need to modify the component syntax slightly.

>
> From this I take it that your "\theta" in the earlier model definition
> is this precision parameter, so that it's just a single scalar
> parameter?
> Then I think the joint theta,cp1,cp2 model should be doable as an
> generic model, with \theta parameterised as a quantile transformation
> of a variable v.
> For example, let the prior distributions be
> v ~ N(0,1)
> log_cp1 ~ LogGamma(...)
> log_cp2 ~ LogGamma(...)
> Then, when constructing Q, you'd just transform v into it's intended
> Ga(cp1,cp2) distribution for the precision (theta):
> Q <- Diagonal(n, x = qgamma(pnorm(v), shape = exp(log_cp1), rate =
> exp(log_cp2))
>
> For a more numerically stable construction, use the
> inlabru::bru_forward_transformation() method:
> inlabru::bru_forward_transformation(qgamma, v, shape = exp(log_cp1),
> rate = exp(log_cp2))
> This uses al the internal log=TRUE and log.p=TRUE options in the pnorm
> and qgamma functions, so that the transformation is well-defined in
> the distribution tails.
>
> I'm not entirely convinced that you can actually get useful estimates
> of cp1 and cp2 out of this model though; not due to inla limitations,

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Reference/Baseline in INLA
messages.body_plain:
its the model.matrix() from lm() that do this, hence it use one of them as a reference value, so the values are relative to the one not there.

it will not help having all as then the marginal stdev will be very very high, as only differences are likelihood identifiable.

There is always an option to rewrite this differently, if you *have*to* have all values, like this, where you instead of having a reference level
you a sum-to-zero-constraint

n=12
> y=rnorm(n)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] BLUP and BLUE estimation
messages.body_plain:
the small changes are due to the parallel computations

I see you have turned off the intercept term, hence it will be captured
in the spde term (likely). so if you're data is far from mean zero, then
the range will be elevated due to this.

you can make sure the above will happen, adding

	f(clone, model="iid", constr=TRUE)

which will force this term to sum-to-zero

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to define covariates with temporal variations in inlabru?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] How to define covariates with temporal variations in inlabru?
messages.body_plain:
It depends a bit on the observation/likelihood setting. For
point-referenced data (counts at specific locations, and similar), you
can either use the
 covar(covar_object, model=...)
or
 covar(covar_object, main_layer = "bathymetry", model=...)
approach (the first one assumes you want the first layer, or one
called "covar", like the component name). The latter is equivalent to
 bathymetry(covar_object, model=...)
Or store the covariate values in the data object together with the
other measurements.
For point process models, the covariate needs to be available
everywhere, and then you need the first approach, since you don't know
where the covariate will need to be evaluated by the likelihood
approximation construction.
Whether time is involved or not just affects whether you need to
specify additional information to extract different columns for
different time points.
In the inlabru devel version, the selector argument is'nt needed as
much anymore, as we've expanded the main_layer argument to take a
vector from the input data, like time:
 covar(covar_object, main_selector="time", model=...)
can now be written as
  covar(covar_object, main_layer=time, model=...)
instead.  The internal system can also be accessed directly, like for example
  covar(eval_spatial(covar_object, .data, layer = "bathymetry"), model=...)
or
  covar(eval_spatial(covar_object, .data, layer = time), model=...)

A new vignette (still under construction, but mostly done) discusses
more details on component construction:
  https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/components_vignette.html
(the name&link may change in the future)
Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] plotting posterior inference on mesh
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
You can extract the relevant rows of the output for each time point using the information from inla.spde.make.index()
The first second or third vector (depending on how you setup the model, with group or replicate) contains the information about which elements belong to which time point.

Once you’ve done that, you have multiple options, but the inlabru ggplot() support is probably easiest. See ?inlabru::gg
Something like ggplot(result$summary.random$field[index$field.group==1,]) +
  gg(mesh, aes(fill=mean))
(I’m not at computer to check the details right now; see the help page examples that I think includes this)

Finn

messages.subject_clean: Predictions to covariates with a temporal component
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone

So I’ve set up a model like this now:

cmp_temp <- Species ~ mySmooth(coordinates,

                               model = matern, group = SurveyID,

                               control.group = list(model = "iid"),

                               ngroup = 10) +

  SST_mean_effect(main=SSTmean,model="linear") +

  UK_bathymetry_effect(main=UK_bathymetry,model = "linear") +

  UK_bath_slope_effect(main=UK_bath_slope,model="linear") +

  DistShip_effect(main=DistShip,model="linear")+

  DistWF_effect(main=DistWF,model="linear") +

  Intercept(1)

### NOTE - in the above, the temporal component of SST is incorporated into the DATsp dataframe already - this was pre-processed ahead of time.

#######

fit_temp <- bru(components=cmp_temp, data=DATsp, family = "nbinomial",

                options = list(control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb",

                                                   strategy = "simplified.laplace")))

That seems to run.

Now the question is – how do I integrate the temporal SST data so I can make the predictions. At the minute I’ve got this far:

ppxl <- pixels(mesh=mesh, mask = Boundary)

pxlcrds <- data.frame(ppxl@coords)

pxlpts <- sf::st_as_sf(pxlcrds,

                       coords=c("x","y"),

                       crs=UTM30string)

ppxl$DistShip_effect <- as.numeric(sf::st_distance(SLs,pxlpts,which = "Euclidean")[1,])

ppxl$DistWF_effect <- as.numeric(sf::st_distance(WFs,pxlpts,which = "Euclidean")[1,])

ppxl$UK_bathymetry_effect <- over(ppxl,Bathycrop)

ppxl$UK_bath_slope_effect <- over(ppxl,Slopecrop)

ppxl_all <- cprod(ppxl, data.frame(SurveyID = seq_len(10)))

This works fine for the static variables.  But if I’ve got (for example):

SST_surv1 <- as(raster(“Data/mean_SST_surv1.img”), “SpatialPixelsDataFrame”)

SST_surv2 <- as(raster(“Data/mean_SST_surv2.img”), “SpatialPixelsDataFrame”)

…

…

Is there an inlabru / inla  way to incorporate that temporal component?

Cheers

Grant

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] plotting posterior inference on mesh
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

What appears in the linear.predictor output depends on the details of
the model construction, but in general, its
(A \eta, \eta, latent)
and what's in eta and A eta depends on the inla.stack construction.
The A \eta part has the length of the number of observations, and are
the linear predictor values for the observed values, so if you only
care about that part you just need to look at those rows of the
summary.

With 49 stations and 364 days, I'd expect the first 17885 rows to be
your sought linear predictor values.
The length of eta depends on the precise inputs and options for
inla.stack(). Normally it will contain the linear predictor values for
each model component that is directly involved in the A\eta
calculation.
I'd advise against trying to extract/interpret them.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] multicollinearity in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

no, CPO and PIT are unlikely to reveal that by themselves, in
particular if the co-linearity is in fixed effect covariates, since
they measure leave-one-out prediction properties, that tend to be more
sensitive to the observation model and iid&structured latent random
effects.

You'll typically notice effects of co-linearity by the parameter
estimates having wide credible intervals but the combined linear
predictor being more narrow, since co-linearity leads to high
posterior correlation (usually negative) between the parameters.
Whether this is a problem or not depends on the application. For
spatial infill/prediction of the combined effects it is usually not a
problem, since that tends to be well constrained by data even when the
individual effects are not.

Finn

messages.subject: Specifying a Bias Field in INLA
messages.subject_clean: Specifying a Bias Field in INLA
messages.body_plain:
INLA Gurus,
Hello my name is Martin Arostegui. I am a postdoctoral scholar at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution in the USA. I am very recently diving into the world of INLA, integrated species distribution models and so on. I came across this great 2020 paper in Ecography <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/ecog.05146> about different ways of accounting for bias in data collection. The two alternatives it discusses are 1) supplying a bias covariate or 2) including a second spatial field, which appear to be most appropriate when you have some but limited information on bias (but can supply at least one covariate) or effectively no information on bias whatsoever (and then use the second spatial field).

My question is, how might one in R-INLA best go about accounting for bias when you have really good knowledge of the bias distribution and can a priori map it spatially on the same grid as your occurrence data? In my case, I am hoping to use fishery-dependent data that provide a very accurate record of the uneven spatial effort distribution of the fishing fleet for over 20 yrs. I have been searching the relevant literature and the paper above comes closest to what I am aiming to do but I am hoping to more explicitly include a mapped bias field to better inform my integrated species distribution model and decrease its sensitivity to biases of the individual underlying datasets (particularly uneven spatial effort). Any insight you would be willing to share on how this is coded in R-INLA would be greatly appreciated and of enormous help!

Many Thanks,
Martin

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Specifying a Bias Field in INLA
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Specifying a Bias Field in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi Martin,

I think you mostly already answered your own question (apart from the
coding details). If you have a spatial field estimate (with spatially
varying mean and variance, and assuming some simple correlation
structure),
of the predictor bias, you can include the mean as a fixed offset in
the predictor, and add a random field component with the given
correlation (spde=inla.spde2.pcmatern() with prior.sigma=c(1,NA)) and
scaling weights given by the estimated bias standard deviation
(assuming bias_sigma and bias_mean have been evaluated at the
observation locations):
~ ... + f(bias_field, bias_sigma, model=spde) + offset(bias_mean)

In inlabru it would be similar (with all the make.A and inla.stack
code done internally):
~ ... + bias_field(coordinates, bias_sigma, model=spde) +
bias_mean(bias_mean, model="offset")

If the bias estimate is on the observation scale you'd need to work
out what that implies for the predictor and modified observation
model.
There are too many possibilities to say how to do that.

However, note that the likely effect of the above approach is
increased and complicated uncertainty, since the bias field and field
of interest can't be mutually identified; only their sum.
That may be what you need, but it also might not be...

Finn

On Friday, October 21, 2022 at 8:59:01 AM UTC-4 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Martin,
>
> I think you mostly already answered your own question (apart from the
> coding details). If you have a spatial field estimate (with spatially
> varying mean and variance, and assuming some simple correlation
> structure),
> of the predictor bias, you can include the mean as a fixed offset in
> the predictor, and add a random field component with the given
> correlation (spde=inla.spde2.pcmatern() with prior.sigma=c(1,NA)) and
> scaling weights given by the estimated bias standard deviation
> (assuming bias_sigma and bias_mean have been evaluated at the
> observation locations):
> ~ ... + f(bias_field, bias_sigma, model=spde) + offset(bias_mean)
>
> In inlabru it would be similar (with all the make.A and inla.stack
> code done internally):
> ~ ... + bias_field(coordinates, bias_sigma, model=spde) +
> bias_mean(bias_mean, model="offset")
>
> If the bias estimate is on the observation scale you'd need to work
> out what that implies for the predictor and modified observation
> model.
> There are too many possibilities to say how to do that.
>
> However, note that the likely effect of the above approach is
> increased and complicated uncertainty, since the bias field and field
> of interest can't be mutually identified; only their sum.
> That may be what you need, but it also might not be...
>
> Finn
>
> On Thu, 20 Oct 2022 at 14:54, MARTIN AROSTEGUI
> <martin.a...@whoi.edu> wrote:
> >
> > INLA Gurus,
> > Hello my name is Martin Arostegui. I am a postdoctoral scholar at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution in the USA. I am very recently diving into the world of INLA, integrated species distribution models and so on. I came across this great 2020 paper in Ecography about different ways of accounting for bias in data collection. The two alternatives it discusses are 1) supplying a bias covariate or 2) including a second spatial field, which appear to be most appropriate when you have some but limited information on bias (but can supply at least one covariate) or effectively no information on bias whatsoever (and then use the second spatial field).
> >
> > My question is, how might one in R-INLA best go about accounting for bias when you have really good knowledge of the bias distribution and can a priori map it spatially on the same grid as your occurrence data? In my case, I am hoping to use fishery-dependent data that provide a very accurate record of the uneven spatial effort distribution of the fishing fleet for over 20 yrs. I have been searching the relevant literature and the paper above comes closest to what I am aiming to do but I am hoping to more explicitly include a mapped bias field to better inform my integrated species distribution model and decrease its sensitivity to biases of the individual underlying datasets (particularly uneven spatial effort). Any insight you would be willing to share on how this is coded in R-INLA would be greatly appreciated and of enormous help!
> >

> > Martin

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] problem with joint model of BYM and SPDE
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] problem with joint model of BYM and SPDE
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

One spatial effect is defined at the mesh nodes while the other is defined at the areal id. In order to share one of them in the linear predictor where the other is primarily used, you need to do some "projection" into the other "model domain". Both will have to use the 'copy' feature in INLA. Either you have to "collect" the areal level effect for point referred observation or to project the continuous domain effect from the mesh nodes into the areal level. There are technical implication details and assumptions at the linear predictor level for the latter. Thus *one way* would be to copy the bym model to the linear predictor for the point referred data model. All you need is to create an index for each data location identifying which area it belongs to and use it as f(id.point.area, copy='area', ...) where 'area' is the name of the index for the bym model. In order to implement it in plain inla you may have to use inla.stack() for the areal data and merge both data stacks. This would be easier using inlabru.

best regards,
Elias

messages.body_plain:
I am going fit a spatio-temporal model for areal data.
The data and the code used to implement the model is given below:
### import the data (give the exact directory of the excel data from your computer)
M_Dat <- read.csv("C:/Users/user/Desktop/Gezahegn.csv")

### Import the shapefile ()

library(spData)
library(sp)
library(PROJ)
library(geos)
library(sf)
library(spdep)
shapef <- st_read("C:/Users/user/Desktop/shapefile/Amhara_woreda_recent_boundary.shp")

### Generating spatial weight matrix in R-INLA

temp <- poly2nb(shapef)
nb2INLA("Amhara.graph", temp)
Amhara_shape <- paste(getwd(),"/Amhara.graph",sep="")
Amhara_shape

## Type I interaction

## Type I interaction: Model specification

Type_I<-Y~X1+X2+X3+X4+X5+X6+X7+X8+X9+X10+X11
+f(FiD1,model="bym",graph=Amhara_shape,hyper = list(prec.unstruct=list(prior="loggamma",param=c(1,0.001)),
prec.spatial=list(prior="loggamma",param=c(1,0.001)))) +
f(Month_1,model="rw2") +
f(Month_2,model="iid") +
f(FiD.T,model="iid")

Mod_I<- inla(formula =Type_I, family ="gpoisson",data=M_Dat,offset=Pop,
control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
control.compute=list(config=TRUE,cpo=TRUE,dic=TRUE,waic=TRUE))

summary(Mod_I)

Mod_I_2 <- inla(formula =Type_I, family ="nbinomial",data=M_Dat,offset=Pop,
control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
control.compute=list(config=TRUE,cpo=TRUE,dic=TRUE,waic=TRUE))

summary(Mod_I_2)

messages.subject: problems with ipoints() and inla.spTransform() when using S^2 mesh in Cartesian xyz
messages.subject_clean: problems with ipoints() and inla.spTransform() when using S^2 mesh in Cartesian xyz
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Apologies if this is a trivial enquiry. I am a new user to
INLA and have been trying to use inlabru::ipoints(samplers, domain,…) to
generate integration points.

Our samplers is a SpatialPolygonsDataFrame (called “sp”) in
lat-lon coordinates, and the domain is an inla.mesh object (called “mesh1”) on
the sphere (S^2) in Cartesian geocentric xyz coordinates. The reason that our
mesh is in Cartesian xyz is we are modelling global processes, so our mesh has
to be on S^2. We find we have to supply loc= Cartesian, geodetic xyz
coordinates to inla.mesh.2d() to make meshes with full global coverage (i.e. to
have longitude-wrapping and equal area). The inla.mesh.2d function seems to
project lon-lat locations onto R^2.

When I ran ipoints(samplers=sp, domain=mesh1, group=”index”),
I got the error “sp::over(samplers, integ_sp, returnList = TRUE) :
identicalCRS(x, y) is not TRUE”. Then I tried to use inla.spTransform(mesh1,
inla.CRS("longlat")) to make mesh1 have the same CRS as the
SpatialPolygons, but I got the error “'crs0' is an invalid coordinate reference
object”.

Does anyone know whether inla transformation function is possible
to transform a S^2 mesh object in Cartesian xyz to a S^2 mesh in lon-lat? If it
is possible, what would be the correct way to do that?

Thank you very much. Any guidance will be much appreciated!

Best wishes,

Xueqing

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] problems with ipoints() and inla.spTransform() when using S^2 mesh in Cartesian xyz
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] problems with ipoints() and inla.spTransform() when using S^2 mesh in Cartesian xyz
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The ipoints function doesn't have full support for global meshes yet,
as it relies on conversion to a flat equal-area projection to compute
the integration weights.
I hope to soon have a new ipoints version to properly support this use case.

What kind of region is your sampler? What coordinate system is it stored in?
It's possible this issue can't be fully solved until we get more of
the more general sf support working.

For debugging purposes only:
Can you please try the mesh transformation with
inlabru::fm_spTransform() instead of inla.spTransform() and let me
know if that makes a difference or not?
It wouldn't give a usable mesh, but it should be able to do the
coordinate transformation.

A potential workaround would be to make an integration scheme for the
entire mesh, with the mesh nodes as integration points; something like
this:

ips_sphere <- SpatialPointsDataFrame(mesh$loc, data=data.frame(
    weight = inla.mesh.fem(mesh)$va * earth.radius^2
  ), crs = fm_CRS("sphere"))
ips_globe <- fm_spTransform(ips_sphere, fm_CRS("globe"))

and then filter out the points outside the polygon, with a direct call
to sp::over.  That way, the mesh wouldn't need to be involved in the
coordinate transformations.

For full integration accuracy along the sampler boundary, this step
needs to be done before aggregating the integration points, but it
might be sufficient as a temporary workaround.

I'll put this as an inlabru github issue to keep track of it.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

Thank you so much
for the quick response. We will try the potential workaround as suggested.

Our sampler is a
SpatialPolygonDataframe. Each row in the data is a polygon area, and the
observation values are area-averages over a polygon area. The coordinate
reference system is “+proj=longlat +ellps=WGS84”. Here I attached an example
for simulating our sampler.

In addition, I
just realized that the coordinate reference system (crs) information for our
mesh was somehow left out and so mesh$crs is NULL. After clearly specifying a
CRS to the mesh, both inlabru::fm_spTransform() and inla.spTransform() are able
to do the coordinate transformation.

Best wishes,

Xueqing

The mesh transformation may _run_, but the resulting mesh isn't usable
for _correct_ computations, as it becomes a deformed flattened mesh
that folds in on itself.
The correct solution is to transform and calculate on the sphere
instead of in projections; no projection handles the full globe
properly.

I have a PhD student who's working on polygon-aggregated data
problems, and coe for this will be making its way into the package.

Finn

> >> Hi,
> >>
> >> The ipoints function doesn't have full support for global meshes yet,
> >> as it relies on conversion to a flat equal-area projection to compute
> >> the integration weights.
> >> I hope to soon have a new ipoints version to properly support this use case.
> >>
> >> What kind of region is your sampler? What coordinate system is it stored in?
> >> It's possible this issue can't be fully solved until we get more of
> >> the more general sf support working.
> >>
> >> For debugging purposes only:
> >> Can you please try the mesh transformation with
> >> inlabru::fm_spTransform() instead of inla.spTransform() and let me

> >> It wouldn't give a usable mesh, but it should be able to do the
> >> coordinate transformation.
> >>
> >> A potential workaround would be to make an integration scheme for the
> >> entire mesh, with the mesh nodes as integration points; something like
> >> this:
> >>
> >> ips_sphere <- SpatialPointsDataFrame(mesh$loc, data=data.frame(
> >> weight = inla.mesh.fem(mesh)$va * earth.radius^2
> >> ), crs = fm_CRS("sphere"))
> >> ips_globe <- fm_spTransform(ips_sphere, fm_CRS("globe"))
> >>
> >> and then filter out the points outside the polygon, with a direct call
> >> to sp::over. That way, the mesh wouldn't need to be involved in the
> >> coordinate transformations.
> >>
> >> For full integration accuracy along the sampler boundary, this step
> >> needs to be done before aggregating the integration points, but it
> >> might be sufficient as a temporary workaround.

messages.body_plain:
The fitted values for the Poisson

y ~ Poisson(E * exp(eta))

will be

fitted.values = exp(eta)

note that 'E' is NOT included.

like this:

> r=inla(y ~ 1, data=data.frame(y=200,E=2), E=E, family="poisson", control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE))
> r$summary.fitted.values$mean
[1] 100.247275

while

> r=inla(y ~ 1, data=data.frame(y=200), family="poisson", control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE))
> r$summary.fitted.values$mean
[1] 200.4945483

if you want ``probabilities'' there is no unique way to get those. usually, but not always, then if

y ~ Poisson(E * exp(eta))

this is a shorthand, or an approximation, for

y ~ Binomial(size=N, prob=p)

so you can define

E * eta = N * p

*if* you know what 'N' is

messages.subject: Mismatching row sizes when creating estimation/prediction stacks
messages.subject_clean: Mismatching row sizes when creating estimation/prediction stacks
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA Developers,

I am adapting code from the spatio-temporal analysis conducted by Paula Moraga in Ch. 10 of her Geospatial Health Data textbook <https://www.paulamoraga.com/book-geospatial/sec-geostatisticaldataexamplest.html#stack-with-data-for-estimation-and-prediction-2>. My goal is to predict seroprevalence in Haiti to malaria based on time (survey year), spatial effects, and a set of covariates using georeferenced point data; as a reminder, in her analysis, she predicted levels of air pollution in Spain, also using point data.

I was able to use Dr. Moraga's code for my own data, up until the time came to create the prediction and estimation stacks.

For reference, my prediction dataset looks like this, with 130,940 rows corresponding to 32,735 georeferenced points per year:

Any covariate values with a temporal component (e.g., rain) correspond to the average for that set of coordinates in the year indicated, while static covariate values (e.g., elevation) unique to each location are simply repeated across each year for that location. It is unlikely that different coordinates were included in each year based on the method I used to obtain these covariate values (using sample raster values in QGIS).

My observation dataset has the same structure, with 1,120 rows corresponding to 1,120 locations, which were surveyed once in a given year (2014, 2015, 2016, or 2017).

However, when I attempt to create estimation and prediction stacks, I get the following error code for both:

Can you please let me know how I might be able to resolve this error?

This is the code I used for the stacks, if it helps:

I truly appreciate any help or guidance.

Thank you,

Alicia

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Mismatching row sizes when creating estimation/prediction stacks
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The error message indicates that there is a size mismatch between your covariate effects and the number of rows in the A-matrix.
You didn’t say which of the two stacks gives the error, but I suggest checking the inputs to both stack calls. For the first call, the data.frame for the covariates newest to have the same number of rows as the A matrix. For the second call the data.frame needs to match the number of rows in Ap.

Finn

messages.subject: INLA Crash with ePower package
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am running Windows 10 and up-to-date versions of R and RStudio. I am working on a power analysis for a BACI experiment with the epower package. When I try to use the fitData( ) function to bring in an .xlsx file I get an error message that the INLA program (which is a package dependency) has crashed. I have scoured help boards and none of the solutions have worked for me. Part of the issue is that I don't know how to manipulate inla arguments through the functions of a different package.

The code, which is quite short, is reproduced below and the input file is attached. FWIW, I have not had this problem when running the exact same code on macOS Big Sur (11.6). I am attempting to run the code on a windows desktop machine to avoid having the long run time of the code on my personal laptop.

Thank you for any thoughts.

##### BACI Power Analysis #####

rm(list=ls())

.libPaths("C:/Program Files/R/R-4.2.2rc/library") #set library path for install packages

#install three packages that are dependencies for epower
install.packages("doParallel")
install.packages("XLConnect")
install.packages("INLA", repos=c(getOption("repos"), INLA="https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/stable"), dep=TRUE)

library(doParallel)
library(XLConnect)
library(INLA)

#download epower package from .tar.gz file (link below) and install using Install Packages (under Tools) in RStudio

#https://github.com/bmtglobal/epower/blob/master/epower_1.3.tar.gz
library(epower)

#run analysis
fitData() #brings in .xlsx data ---> INLA CRASH HAPPENING AT THIS STEP

assessPower() #runs power analysis

######## end of code ##########

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Boundary constraints in spatial models
messages.body_plain:
With control.inla you would need a separate likelihood for the special
"observations".
But there's also a "scale" parameter to inla() itself, that _might_ be
useful, in that you can set a large scaling factor for the precision
for those particular "observations".
However, since they will still be involved in the parameter
estimation, I would worry that they would influence the precision
estimates too much, so the multi-likelihood options seems much safer.

You just need to make the observation variable a matrix.
Instead of y = c(ordinary_obs, special_obs), use
y=rbind(cbind(ordinary_obs, NA), cbind(NA, special_obs)) .
(that's for plain inla; in inlabru, that matrix is constructed
automatically when building multi-likelihood models, so you don't need
the NA stuff there).

Then
  family = c("gaussian", "gaussian")
and
  control.family = list(list(...), list(...))
containing the two separate hyper-definitions.

Finn
